The screen is LANDSCAPE, 448×368. The panel is wired portrait and the firmware rotates it 270°, so landscape is what anyone ever sees and a “368×448” anywhere is backwards. The app's 240×200 panel is this proportion.

A face is data. One JSON file per set in design-system/faces/ holds per-state geometry, colour, gaze, per-eye asymmetry and motion, and the firmware's C, the app's Kotlin, 32 notification drawables, the prototype's React and this card are all generated from it. 4 sets ship — Classic, Bloom, Little Computer, Pixel — switchable at runtime and kept by the pet. Every state of every set is drawn in the Pet faces cards, from the same JSON; these five are classic, the fallback.

Eyes and mouth are strokes along arcs. A mouth is a chord, a thickness and a bulge — positive smiles, negative frowns, zero is the flat capsule every face was before curves existed — and an eye curves the same way, which is what draws the “^ ^”. The radius and both angles are derived once, in the generator, so four renderers cannot curve differently.

Sick is not a variation on sad. They mean different things and demand different actions — feed me versus put the phone down — so they must not be confusable across a room. The generator refuses a set whose sad and sick share eyes or share a mouth.

It is never themed, and it is not one colour either. This is a picture of a switched-on AMOLED, so it does not follow the phone's light or dark setting. It follows the set: eye, mouth, panel, text and control are the set's own, checked against a WCAG floor and a ceiling so the pet is readable across a room and the talk button never shouts louder than the face.

Three states are the pet's alone. sleepy and surprised are written by the phone, decay on the device and are never reported back; asleep is the pet's own. The phone draws the baseline rather than guessing — never assert what we have not been told.
